newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco talks recess, FDA powers an issue.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco talks recess, FDA powers an issue.

text.p: A tobacco settlement meeting of industry representatives and state attorneys general recessed Tuesday with the question of Food and Drug Administration authority at issue.

Negotiators said that while the larger meeting ended, smaller groups would remain in Washington to work on separate issues. They said another meeting with the industry representatives could be set next week.
Steven Parrish, Philip Morris Cos Inc. senior vice president of corporate affairs, said the scheduling of another large meeting would rest on whether progress was made among the smaller groups.
"Depending on how that goes, we'll decide if it makes sense to get the big group together again," he said.
A telephone conference call among the attorneys general that have sued the tobacco industry is scheduled for Wednesday morning.
About 35 attorneys general, the highest ranking legal officers of each state, have sued the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid health care costs of smokers.

The states, along with plaintiffs lawyers who have filed class action lawsuits and members of the health community, have been negotiating with the industry since early April to try to resolve mounting litigation against cigarette makers.
The complex talks have been snagged on numerous issues and several negotiators said sessions held late Monday night and Tuesday concerned the FDA's authority to regulate cigarettes.
Washington state Attorney General Christine Gregoire said some industry representatives were concerned that the FDA would someday try to ban cigarettes completely.
"We want to make sure the FDA regulates nicotine as a drug. We're not backing off from it," said Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, a key negotiator in the talks.
Attorneys general involved in the talks appeared exhausted after meeting until 2 a.m. Tuesday and resuming sessions later in the morning.

Moore has been trying to reach a deal ahead of the July 7 trial date in his state's case against the industry. The Mississippi case is scheduled to be the first of the state Medicaid suits to go to trial, followed by Florida and Texas.
Although Moore has remained optimistic throughout the negotiations, he acknowledged that the talks were "tough" but still hoped to reach a deal.
"We're making good progress. I contemplate we're going to bring this to a final resolution pretty soon," Moore said.
He said he was planning to brief public health, congressional members and others during the next few days "in an attempt to build support."

"There are final details to be worked out. We still have some contentious issues with the industry. The attorneys general have taken very strong positions on certain issues. We are not moving from our positions," he said.

Separately, two leading public health advocates wrote to President Bill Clinton asking that the White House "refrain from taking a position on any proposed new tobacco control legislation that might emerge from the settlement talks until the public health community has had sufficient time and opportunity to examine and consider the implications."

The letter was signed by former Surgeon General C. Everett Koop and former FDA Commissioner David Kessler on behalf of an advisory committee on public health and tobacco set up by some members of Congress.
